historical_timeline.summary: First major league game, for the Brooklyn Dodgers.
Retirement from baseball announced; diabetes diagnosed at about this time.
Nerve and artery damage in his legs by this year.
His eldest son killed in an automobile accident.
Nearly blind, walking with a cane, grieving the deaths of his mentor, mother and son.
Died of a heart attack at his home in Stamford, Connecticut, at 53.

claims.statement: Jackie Robinson was born on January 31, 1919, in Cairo, Georgia, to a family of sharecroppers.
On April 15, 1947, he played his first major league game for the Brooklyn Dodgers, ending more than sixty years of segregation in major league baseball.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Anchors his identity and his long experience of public pressure in the modern social history.

claims.statement: His retirement from baseball was announced in January 1957; he then worked in business and as a spokesman and fundraiser for civil rights causes, including the NAACP.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Anchors his later working life in the modern social history.

claims.statement: He had diabetes and high blood pressure; his death is attributed to heart problems and complications of diabetes.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The anchor for the modern diabetes, hypertension and cardiovascular risk. The type and treatment of his diabetes are not given in the sources consulted.

claims.statement: He was diagnosed with diabetes at about 37, around the time he retired from baseball, and at first kept it private; two of his brothers also had diabetes.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Anchors the long duration of diabetes and the family history. Other accounts give other years, and one source says he acknowledged it only a few years after retiring.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Sight-, heart-, limb- and kidney-protecting care for a 52-year-old Black man with long-standing type 2 diabetes who comes in with blurred vision six weeks after the death of his son. The episode covers urgent retina care for proliferative diabetic retinopathy with macular edema and a vitreous hemorrhage (dilated examination, OCT, intravitreal anti-VEGF injections and panretinal photocoagulation, as the AAO Preferred Practice Pattern describes); lowering glucose steadily rather than quickly, with the early worsening of retinopathy after rapid A1c falls and after semaglutide explained and a GLP-1 receptor agonist started only after the retina is stable; an SGLT2 inhibitor for heart and kidney protection; a high-intensity statin with ezetimibe; blood pressure and kidney care; coronary disease found through exertional chest tightness; the ankle-brachial index, foot examination and wound care for a neuropathic heel blister; low-vision services and diabetes tools he can use with poor sight; depression screening and grief support; and the equity of care for a Black man with diabetes complications, under the ADA Standards of Care 2026, the AAO Diabetic Retinopathy Preferred Practice Pattern 2025, the 2024 ACC/AHA PAD and 2023 chronic coronary disease guidelines, and the CMID monographs.

visit_schedule.purpose: Visit for blurred vision and new floaters, chest tightness on stairs, calf pain on walking and numb feet, in a man with long-standing diabetes six weeks after the death of his son
Review after the retina consultation and first eye injections: retinal diagnosis, glucose, blood pressure and kidney medicines
Same-day sick visit for a blister on the right heel, and review of the stress test result
Four weeks after the new medicines: potassium and creatinine, blood pressure, ankle-brachial index, feet, mood, and the second eye injections
Three-month review: A1c, urine albumin, lipids, eyes after laser treatment, heart, legs, grief, and a GLP-1 receptor agonist

assessment.assessment: High-risk proliferative retinopathy in both eyes with center-involving macular edema and reduced vision in both. Anti-VEGF injections treat both the edema and the new vessels and are the first treatment; panretinal photocoagulation adds durable control of the proliferative disease and lessens the burden of frequent injections, and is done when the view allows
From the new vessels; the retina is attached and there is no traction, so vitrectomy is not needed now. Most such hemorrhages clear over weeks with anti-VEGF treatment

Better glucose control will protect his eyes over years, but a very rapid fall in A1c can worsen proliferative retinopathy for a time, and semaglutide was associated with more retinopathy complications in a cardiovascular outcomes trial, mainly in people with existing retinopathy and large early A1c falls. A steady fall of about one point every three months is reasonable, and a GLP-1 receptor agonist can be started once the proliferative disease is controlled, with monthly retina review. An SGLT2 inhibitor raises no retinal concern

Panretinal photocoagulation to the right eye once the hemorrhage clears enough to allow it, and to the left eye if new vessels persist after the first injections
Vitrectomy if the right hemorrhage does not clear within one to three months, or if a retinal detachment develops
Continue aspirin 81 mg: it does not increase the risk or severity of vitreous hemorrhage in diabetic retinopathy, and he needs it after his strokes

Lower the A1c gradually, about one point every three months; delay a GLP-1 receptor agonist until I judge the retina stable, then start at the lowest dose with monthly retina review; an SGLT2 inhibitor and blood pressure and lipid treatment can go ahead now
Low-vision evaluation now (magnifiers, lighting, phone and computer voice tools), a talking glucose meter and an insulin pen with audible clicks; he should not drive until acuity is reassessed
